classification.difficultyReason: Requires recognising the inverse-existence condition and justifying equivalence using composition in both directions.

content.prompt: Is solving $f(f(x))=x$ the same as solving $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ in general?

answer.short: Only when the inverse function $f^{-1}$ exists, with the expressions defined. Otherwise, $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ is not a defined equation.
answer.worked:
Suppose $f^{-1}$ exists. Applying $f^{-1}$ to $f(f(x))=x$ gives $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$, using $f^{-1}(f(u))=u$.

Conversely, applying $f$ to $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ gives $f(f(x))=x$, using $f(f^{-1}(x))=x$. Thus the equations have the same solutions on their valid domains.

If $f$ is not one-to-one, its inverse function does not exist, so the second equation is undefined.
